d73fea9cfa8ca79997ddcfd4.title_original: The 3DS Oracle: BIN Attack via the Network
d73fea9cfa8ca79997ddcfd4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EMV 3-D Secure (3DS) requires a client-visible continuation boundary in browser-mediated flows; in some deployments, that boundary exposes a pre-authorization classification channel. This paper studies 3DS as a protocol, integration surface, and governance problem, combining standards analysis, architectural reconstruction, formal modeling, a documentation audit, disclosure history, and a bounded live evaluation. We show that client-visible integrations can reflect routing and authentication state before financial authorization, allowing 3DS to function as a profiling and screening channel for issuer controls and cardholder/account state rather than only as a defense. In the tested browser-channel Braintree/Cardinal path, the first client-visible result separated researcher-owned anchor cards from bounded adjacent same-range comparison PANs in six of seven distinct ACS/card-range cohorts; separate public evidence, including openly accessible attacker tooling, rotating-proxy support, and illicit paid 3DS card-testing services, shows that comparable signals are already operationalized in the wild. Our live study was deliberately bounded for ethical reasons, so the empirical ceiling reported here reflects researcher restraint rather than an attacker-side scalability limit, although we do not claim network-wide prevalence or candidate issuance. The deeper issue is systemic: decoupled pre-authorization authentication, weak requestor-

0a3741a3613df1592c92f941.title_original: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, and Mixers on Ethereum
0a3741a3613df1592c92f941.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Illicit actors exploit Ethereum's deep liquidity and diverse on-chain services to launder criminal proceeds by combining decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, cross-chain bridges, and mixers in multi-stage processes. Existing anti-money laundering tracing methods fail to disentangle the underlying asset-flow paths in complex transactions, potentially misdirecting subsequent tracing; cannot identify cross-chain intent without pre-collected bridge information; and treat mixers as generic exit services, overlooking post-mixer laundering flows. We present FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets across Ethereum services. First, we propose a method based on the Context-Aware Transfer Tree (CATT) to recover intra-transaction asset-flow paths, which guide accurate tracing and service analysis. Second, we extract discriminative features from asset-flow and execution-evidence perspectives and train a classifier to identify transactions with cross-chain intent. Third, we leverage evidence from the upstream laundering network to analyze potential post-mixer laundering activities. Evaluation on 20 real-world laundering cases demonstrates FPTracer's effectiveness. It achieves the highest recall for both known laundering addresses (98.6%) and destinations (94.2%). It identifies all known uses of bridges in these cases and uncovers 30 previously unreported ones. Among 18 cases with identified Tornado Cash usage, FPTracer can identify

752917d710ab7689f62e050c.title_original: Automated Post-Exploitation Attack Chain Exploration Based on a Phase-guided Hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search Algorithm
752917d710ab7689f62e050c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advanced attackers in post-exploitation scenarios increasingly craft attack chains that combine benign operations, configuration errors, and vulnerability exploitation to achieve objectives like privilege escalation. While such chains pose significant threats, manually discovering them in complex modern host environments is prohibitively labor-intensive. Automating this discovery is therefore essential for proactive defense, yet existing methods still suffer from inefficiency and lack diversity when exploring these attack chains. To address these limitations, we present APEX, an Automated Post-EXploitation attack chain exploration system. This system transforms attack chain discovery into a planning problem and solves it with a novel phase-guided hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm. By organizing attack actions into semantic phases and integrating symbolic planning with MCTS, APEX enables efficient exploration of the state space while generating multiple diverse chains. Evaluations on a benchmark comprising 5 virtual machines, 30 synthetic problems and 291 cloud instances demonstrate that APEX successfully discovers both known and previously unreported attack chains--including 9 novel privilege escalation vectors--providing actionable intelligence for hardening complex production environments.

5996c4583e9b99675755c2a6.title_original: Embedding Large PQC KEMs in IKEv2
5996c4583e9b99675755c2a6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms carry public keys far larger than the established VPN handshake protocol IKEv2 was designed for. At the same time, its initial exchange comprising the public keys cannot be fragmented. In response, the IETF discusses a range of protocol adjustments, yet these proposals have never been compared in terms of their performance and stability under identical conditions. We systematically screened the IETF document corpus for such proposals, added three of our own (one using forward error correction and two using IKEv2 with QUIC, namely QUIKE and QUIKE with a composite key exchange), identified two specification gaps in existing acknowledgment drafts, and implemented all eight on the same open-source codebase. Measurements across different bandwidths, latencies, and packet loss rates, and with ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, and Classic McEliece, total 126 500 handshakes in 1296 different configurations and show that no mechanism fully compensates for the effect of the key size on performance. For Classic McEliece, no approach handles challenging conditions acceptably. The approaches either congest the link or take up to nearly two minutes per handshake on average. For ML-KEM and FrodoKEM, there are two ways forward: building on already standardized extensions or delegating the transport. The former requires the larger implementation change and needs further optimization, such as acknowledgment mechanisms or

13b77c79bfcb9889f32d6c71.title_original: On Task, Off Track: Benchmarking LLM and Agent Robustness to Near-Target Prompt Injection
13b77c79bfcb9889f32d6c71.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt injection benchmarks assess whether large language models (LLMs) and agents resist malicious instructions embedded in external content. However, a system could perform well by rejecting attacks that obviously abandon the user's request, while still accepting changes that retain most of a legitimate answer but make it incorrect or harmful. Testing more instructions for unrelated outcomes would not necessarily reveal this weakness. We call attacks seeking responses designed to resemble legitimate answers while introducing incorrect or harmful changes near-target prompt injection. We introduce NTBench, the Near-Target Benchmark, which builds on legitimate tasks from existing datasets. For each task, a legitimate reference outcome guides the generation of target--instruction pairs, with separate tracks targeting incorrect and harmful outcomes in responses or agent tool invocations. Harmful targets can also accompany otherwise correct task completion. We combine LLM-based checks with human validation of the intended deviations, then assess whether injected instructions induce them using response judgments or tool-call checks, excluding deviations already observed without injection. We evaluate seven LLMs on ten datasets for language tasks and two agent benchmarks. Under a common budget of three attack executions per sample, both tracks achieve higher overall attack success rates than the fixed-target baseline for every evaluat

257ab47e685fb285a5bdbe50.title_original: Privacy-Preserving Federated Loss Exploration for Vision-Based Perception under Non-IID Data
257ab47e685fb285a5bdbe50.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-based image classification models benefit from Federated Learning (FL) across vehicles, however learning accurate models from distributed vehicular cameras is challenging due to data heterogeneity and privacy concerns. To improve performance on non-IID data, advanced FL optimization approaches have emerged that share auxiliary insights, such as client gradient behaviors. While these gradient-guided optimized FL methods improve the model accuracy, their reliance on sharing additional gradient information introduces a previously unexplored privacy vulnerability. In our empirical privacy-leakage experiment, we show that a malicious server can infer clients' label sets from shared guidance matrices under heterogeneous client label distributions (simulated via Dirichlet-based label partitions), between 50% and 84% accuracy. To address this privacy leakage, we propose PPFLex that replaces the central server with three Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) servers to securely compute the global guidance matrix and perform federated averaging under semi-honest and malicious MPC server assumptions. We evaluate PPFLex on widely used traffic-sign classification datasets (e.g., GTSRB and BTSC) as representative autonomous vehicle perception benchmarks, comparing against baselines. Our results show that PPFLex achieves accuracy comparable to the plain-text FedLEx pipeline while preventing privacy leakage, incurring acceptable MPC overh

2d20452eb1bf0de26e880d9e.title_original: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection
2d20452eb1bf0de26e880d9e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe and BME680 ambient sensor, 1-2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection, replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator, a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random row splits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for Random Forest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than label reconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant "normal" predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465), and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on at

79cc1d3a433cea07329b4a6f.title_original: Identity Amortization: Shared Resources and the Cost of Sybil Attacks
79cc1d3a433cea07329b4a6f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sybil defenses commonly price identities by requiring a resource for each one. When one resource can support several identities, an adversary can pay less per identity than the defense intends. We call this identity amortization: a strict reduction in the minimum cost of provisioning identities when resources may be shared, relative to provisioning each one independently. It is a second route to the gap that a Sybil attack exploits. When influence is assigned per identity, a defense calibrated to the nominal price can overestimate the cost of a Sybil threshold by up to the number of identities one resource supports. For any resource catalogue, we give exact tests for when identity amortization occurs, where it begins, and its largest error; a sharing cap below the onset removes it. Because the tests need only prices and capacities, they apply to any defense that admits identities against a shareable resource, telling designers whether the assumed per-identity cost is paid, how wrong it can be, and which intervention restores it most cheaply for honest participants. On published phone-verification prices, per-account estimates overstate provisioning cost 1.6 to 4.3 times; Tor's raised per-address relay limit cut modeled attack cost by 8 to 72%, depending on the address-to-relay price ratio.

87fcae35bfdaf753539ca789.title_original: Developing Security Metrics for Automated Compliance Checking
87fcae35bfdaf753539ca789.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To automatically check for compliance with security-related standards, prose requirements must be translated to technical properties to make them measurable. A multitude of metrics have been proposed in past literature, but they are lacking a systematic methodology for their elicitation. Without such a methodology, metrics remain inconsistent in their data models and abstraction levels, they exhibit considerable overlaps and are difficult to combine to comprehensively cover a standard's requirement. In this paper, we develop a data model for security metrics based on a systematization of compliance requirements, and we propose a methodology for their elicitation. The method is based on an ontology that enables a systematic development of metrics with a comparable degree of abstraction. We also present our initial work on an open-source effort that demonstrates that our approach also supports a collaborative development of metrics.

2ef6cfc5ce7e713a74912803.title_original: EVSEFuzz : A Tool for Automated Testing of Protocol Implementations
2ef6cfc5ce7e713a74912803.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.

98d90ae552bed7d630aa9691.title_original: The Entire Quantum Computer on a Classical Leash
98d90ae552bed7d630aa9691.excerpt: arXiv:2610.31775v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that a classical client with no quantum hardware can use a single untrusted and potentially malicious quantum server as if it were its own trusted quantum computer. Through the server, the client can privately choose and run quantum computations, prepare quantum states, and process quantum states supplied by other parties. It can also keep quantum memory on the server, hidden from the server itself, and use that memory in later computations so its quantum state persists across rounds of interaction. Together, these capabilities let a purely classical party act as a quantum party in a variety of interactive protocols. We expect this virtual quantum computer to be a broadly useful tool. As immediate applications, we resolve two known open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states. Underlying all of these results is a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, which we construct assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors.

c496772f069f4fa2861b65d6.title_original: Curvature-Aware Clipping: Mitigating Bias in DPSGD via Approximate Second-Order Information
c496772f069f4fa2861b65d6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32175v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD) has become the de facto standard for training deep neural networks with rigorous privacy guarantees. However, the utility of DPSGD is constrained by gradient clipping bias and DP noise. While existing work has tried to address these issues, the geometric misalignment caused by clipping bias remains a critical challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework, Curvature-Aware Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (CA-DPSGD), which leverages approximate second-order information to construct an optimal, curvature-aware clipping space. CA-DPSGD integrates a rectified estimator for the curvature matrix and is coupled with an anisotropic noise mechanism to ensure privacy guarantees. Extensive empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art clipping methods.

d94189814b3090517f78ba41.title_original: Depth-Dependent Safety Geometry in Vision-Language Models: Layer-Wise Localization and Bidirectional Refusal Control
d94189814b3090517f78ba41.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are widely deployed, yet the internal mechanisms behind their safety behavior remain poorly understood. We present a lightweight inference-time framework for localizing and manipulating safety-sensitive representations in frozen VLMs, without retraining or modifying parameters. On Qwen3-VL-4B, layer-wise activation divergence analysis reveals non-uniform safety geometry across depth. Causal interventions show that early vision layers support strong bidirectional refusal control through activation steering along a learned safety direction, with unsafe rejection spanning 6%-96%, whereas later layers respond more to activation magnitude scaling and exhibit a substantial safety-selectivity trade-off. Deeper layers remain well separated along the safety direction yet are largely insensitive to steering, distinguishing representational separability from causal controllability. InternVL2.5-4B shows qualitatively similar depth-dependent activation geometry despite differences in layer location and magnitude. Our results expose a white-box, representation-level refusal-bypass attack surface in VLM vision encoders and motivate inference-time stabilization of safety-sensitive representations.

d295b9e8dd65524d13e745a3.title_original: Democratic Accountability for Autonomous Systems: A Legislative Notification Framework and Comparative Institutional Design
d295b9e8dd65524d13e745a3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32226v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: No domestic legislature has ever reviewed a state's decision to authorise an autonomous cyber weapon before it acted. Closing the international attribution gap is necessary but not sufficient for democratic accountability. We formalise the Tripartite Attribution Framework's three attribution levels and add a fourth, non-legal Democratic Accountability level ($A_{dem}$): a 72-hour legislative notification requirement. Scoring six democratic oversight bodies against five adoptability dimensions yields a counter-intuitive result: the statutes granting these bodies privileged access to classified material are often the same statutes withholding particular ongoing operations from them, so at most one could lawfully receive such a notification today, and the carve-out Level 4 needs is required in nearly every jurisdiction rather than only the least-equipped. Retrospective analysis of Stuxnet, NotPetya, and Volt Typhoon shows one pattern: legal attribution resolvable, domestic democratic review absent.

72b98d8ab1683d6e9e3776cd.title_original: Autonomous Cyber Weapons as AI-Enabled Digital Harms: A Platform Accountability Framework
72b98d8ab1683d6e9e3776cd.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Governments govern AI-generated online harms from commercial platforms (EU DSA, AI Act, UK Online Safety Act), yet the most severe class remains ungoverned: autonomous cyber weapons (ACWs) deployed by nation-states against civilian infrastructure. We address this gap with three contributions: a digital-harm taxonomy (six ACW modes $\times$ five harm categories); the Meaningful Human Control (MHC) Model, a governance-compliance function with a closed-form IHL threshold and a proved weight-sensitivity bound; and a platform accountability architecture with treaty language grounded in ARSIWA state-responsibility doctrine, not Rome Statute individual responsibility. Applied to eleven documented state-attributed operations and one hypothetical defensive AI system, every documented case falls in an accountability vacuum; the threshold is target-dependent, and against wholly civilian targets no system studied clears it, including the hypothetical. Three further incidents are correctly excluded on autonomy/attribution grounds, a discriminant-validity check. The weights and threshold parameters are illustrative, not fitted.

f9b53d8a16f49a576fe1f532.title_original: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
f9b53d8a16f49a576fe1f532.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a critical defense against software security flaws, aiming to triage and fix bugs autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden--either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors--making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework for end-to-end AVR that performs deep analysis by transforming intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. DeepAVR decomposes repair into specialized roles--Fault Localization, Patch Generation, Compile Validation, Security Validation, Functionality Validation, and Patch Review--and routes feedback across these roles to iteratively refine both localization and patch hypotheses. In particular, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, which treats execution results from intermediate patches as diagnostic signals to uncover hidden root causes, and a root-cause-oriented patch review stage that detects symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs beyond execution-based validation. Evaluation on the real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset VulnLoc shows that DeepAVR significantly outperforms prior methods, g

562fbe1d89e4b81528f382bb.title_original: Iterative Behavioral Identification for Covert Misappropriation Attacks
562fbe1d89e4b81528f382bb.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32662v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a data-driven, three-phase framework for covert misappropriation attacks on closed-loop networked control systems. A man-in-the-middle (MITM) adversary, with access only to intercepted input-output data, incrementally identifies the plant's behavioral subspace while maintaining stealth under an infinity-norm intrusion-detection system (IDS). Phase 1 collects an initial rank-deficient Hankel matrix using a low-amplitude probing signal that satisfies an analytical stealth bound. Phase 2 adapts online rank-increasing experiment design to the closed-loop setting, using causal predictor-based masking to limit IDS residuals while the Hankel rank grows from 1 to the full behavioral rank n + mL in exactly n + mL - 1 steps. We show that the identified subspaces are strictly nested and that the projection error of any desired trajectory decreases monotonically, strictly so almost surely at each rank increase. Phase 3 employs the final Hankel matrix in a DeePC-style optimization to synthesize a covert attack that tracks an arbitrary reference while respecting the IDS constraint. Simulations on a DC motor with PI control demonstrate full-rank identification and stealthy tracking. Stealth is guaranteed analytically in Phases 1 and 3 and is numerically supported in Phase 2. The method is model-free and assumes noise-free LTI dynamics.

1adc1441d5eff3f6c83abe24.title_original: Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
1adc1441d5eff3f6c83abe24.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32803v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The consensus protocols of most high-performance blockchains use quorum certificates, which bundle the signatures of a quorum of validators. Signature schemes such as BLS can aggregate the signatures of a whole quorum into a single short signature, which keeps these certificates small. A large-scale quantum computer would break these schemes, and no post-quantum scheme with comparable aggregate size and aggregation time is known. Without aggregation, a certificate holds one large post-quantum signature per member of the quorum, so it becomes infeasible for each validator to broadcast certificates, as modern consensus protocols often require. We present Quantum Cadence, a post-quantum consensus protocol with multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates altogether: every validator counts quorums among the messages it has received itself. Its safety and liveness do not even depend on signatures, although we add signatures to obtain accountability. Quantum Cadence builds on Cadence and replaces its slot consensus, Chorus, with Quantum Chorus, which keeps the optimal fast-path latency of Chorus: dissemination followed by two rounds of votes. When its fast path fails, Quantum Chorus runs Coda, our signature-free Byzantine agreement for multiple proposers. 88607d2c3ed822c34fadf129.title_original: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
88607d2c3ed822c34fadf129.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false ass

759c5acae62d9361fc32fea2.title_original: STROKE: Simple Sparse Structural Occlusions for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
759c5acae62d9361fc32fea2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32932v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce STROKE, a query-efficient score-based black-box adversarial attack that constructs perturbations from simple oriented rectangular occlusions. STROKE optimizes these perturbations through a lightweight greedy add-and-refine procedure. Across diverse image classifiers, STROKE achieves high attack success with low query counts at nominal 1--2\% area settings, showing favorable performance relative to existing patch-based attacks in several configurations. Matched comparisons further demonstrate substantial reductions in wall-clock attack time, while ablation studies examine the key design choices and effectiveness across structural primitives. These findings suggest that simple structural occlusions offer an effective and computationally efficient search space for black-box adversarial attacks.

23c2be40f0494f95d2bf878e.title_original: Differential Fault Analysis of Lilliput under Random-Location Nibble Faults
23c2be40f0494f95d2bf878e.excerpt: arXiv:2603.19781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lilliput is a lightweight block cipher based on a Type-2 Extended Generalized Feistel Network (EGFN). Although it has been studied under conventional cryptanalytic techniques, its resistance to fault attacks remains largely unexplored. We present a theoretical differential fault analysis of Lilliput under a random-location nibble fault model. A nonzero nibble fault is injected at the input to round 27, with the injection location uniformly distributed among the 16 state branches and unknown to the adversary. We analyze fault propagation through the EGFN and derive ciphertext-difference conditions to identify the faulty branch. A DDT-weighted calculation yields an overall branch-identification accuracy of approximately 99.9980% under independent uniform sampling of plaintexts, nonzero fault values, and fault locations; simulations of 2^20 random faults give 99.9983%. After identifying the faulty branch, we classify propagation patterns using the injected difference and the intermediate S-box output difference. We then derive DDT-based constraints on last-round and penultimate-round subkeys and intersect candidate sets from multiple faulty ciphertexts. In 2^15 simulation trials, key-recovery success rates exceed 90%, 95%, and 99% with 32, 36, and 46 faulty ciphertexts, respectively. These simulation-based results are not claims of physical fault-injection performance but offer insight into practical fault analysis of Lilliput.

f9d90a55c8658fec6db2b399.title_original: WebAgentGuard: A Reasoning-Driven Guard Model for Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks in Web Agents
f9d90a55c8658fec6db2b399.excerpt: arXiv:2604.12284v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Web agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) enable autonomous interaction with web environments by perceiving and acting on both visual and textual webpage content to accomplish user-specified tasks. However, they are highly vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in HTML or rendered screenshots can manipulate agent behavior and lead to harmful outcomes such as information leakage. Existing defenses, including system prompt defenses and direct fine-tuning of agents, have shown limited effectiveness. To address this issue, we propose a defense framework in which a web agent operates in parallel with a dedicated guard agent, decoupling prompt injection detection from the agent's own reasoning. Building on this framework, we introduce WebAgentGuard, a reasoning-driven, multimodal guard model for prompt injection detection. We construct a synthetic multimodal dataset using GPT-5 spanning 164 topics and 230 visual and UI design styles, and train the model via reasoning-intensive supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that WebAgentGuard consistently outperforms strong baselines while preserving agent utility, without introducing additional latency.

ee914e1418cf675af9fe0be3.title_original: LocalAlign: Enabling Generalizable Prompt Injection Defense via Generation of Near-Target Adversarial Examples for Alignment Training
ee914e1418cf675af9fe0be3.excerpt: arXiv:2605.01462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly embedded into systems that interact with user data, retrieved web content, and external tools, creating a new attack surface: prompt injection, where malicious commands embedded in untrusted data override the trusted command and induce unintended behavior. Existing defenses mainly rely on fine-tuning the model to preserve an explicit boundary between trusted commands and the untrusted data portion, so that the model learns to prioritize the trusted field and ignore malicious commands in data. However, we observe that while these defenses can block obviously malicious responses caused by injected commands, they generalize poorly to real-world scenarios where the model's response to the injected command is much nearer to the correct response. This is because existing methods typically train against only a fixed set of hand-crafted attack targets, which yields a loose boundary around the correct response and leaves it easier to bypass. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAlign, a more generalizable prompt injection defense inspired by adversarial training. LocalAlign automatically and efficiently generates adversarial examples in which the command embedded in the data portion induces a response that stays near to the correct response while still being wrong. We generate such near-but-wrong adversarial examples using prompting and a single inference step. This design enforces a tight

868020c3273f5a4c0c9c505a.title_original: Block-A-Mole: The Sustainability Frontier of Moving-Target Censorship Resistance
868020c3273f5a4c0c9c505a.excerpt: arXiv:2606.08886v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many censorship circumvention systems keep moving their servers to new cloud addresses, so that whatever the censor discovers soon goes stale. But clients often reach these servers through a name the censor can see and block, such as a hostname or a front domain, and moving a server to a new address does not give it a new name. Existing models treat each proxy as a single unit and leave open when such a system keeps working. We model addresses and names as two coupled layers and ask which one limits availability. Enough servers, rotated fast enough relative to how quickly the censor finds them one at a time, keep some address reachable, and we compute how fast is fast enough. Past that point, faster rotation buys almost nothing, and the names become the limit. If the censor burns names, blocking them for good, $\beta$ times as fast as the system mints new ones, clients can connect less than a $1/\beta$ share of the time, however fast the servers move. For an illustrative system with eight servers and room for eight names, sessions lasting five mean mint intervals stay connected with probability at least 0.95 only while $\beta \leq 0.66$, the system's sustainability frontier, which a censor that times its blocks can cut about tenfold. Public data show that China and Iran block platform names one tenant at a time or a whole suffix at once, that Russia orders such blocks, and that even Snowflake clients need names to obtain pro

b9c7376cdb5c0aa2ac8236e8.title_original: Honeyquest for LLMs: Rethinking Cyber Deception for AI Attackers
b9c7376cdb5c0aa2ac8236e8.excerpt: arXiv:2606.21037v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The empirical foundation of cyber deception relies on human-centered hypotheses, but the rapid emergence of autonomous, AI-enabled attackers challenges whether this foundation transfers to AI agents. To address this, we introduce an automated evaluation framework adapted from the Honeyquest instrument to assess LLM attacker judgment at scale. Our 21-LLM cohort spanned 10 providers, diverse architectures and specializations, open- and closed-weight models, and parameter scales from 8B to over 1T. We evaluated the performance of this LLM cohort (yielding 10,962 responses) against the 47-participant human baseline across an identical set of 174 reconnaissance queries. Our empirical evaluation reveals three key findings that establish LLMs as a distinct attacker class: (1) every model in our cohort falls for deceptive traps at a significantly higher rate than human attackers; (2) the defensive attention-diversion effect observed in humans is statistically absent in our LLM cohort; and (3) a critical recognition-action gap, where LLMs successfully articulate trap recognition in their reasoning but exploit the deceptive elements anyway 73.4% of the time. Across the 21 models, trap recognition in reasoning text did not predict fell-for-trap behavior (Spearman r = +0.08, p = 0.73). Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that human-centered deception hypotheses do not reliably transfer to AI attackers, highlighting the critical need

11a51fcde95c6c8e1a0c397f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.09552v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Regulation such as the EU AI Act requires providers of language models to mark generated text in a machine-readable way. Watermarking meets this requirement by embedding a secret-key signal during generation, so the provider can later detect its model's text. A watermark should stay detectable, preserve quality and survive paraphrasing, but a stronger signal survives more paraphrasing and distorts more text. Providers resolve this trade-off with one configuration for all requests, although a provider may want robustness for misuse-prone requests and no watermark for editing assistance, which the EU AI Act exempts. We introduce \emph{constitution-guided watermarking}, in which the provider states these requirements as natural-language rules, a \emph{watermark constitution}, and each request receives its rule's configuration. Offline, a reasoning agent reads the rules and the watermark code and refines each rule's configuration from measured detection, quality and robustness. At deployment, a monitor routes each prompt to its rule's configuration without modifying the serving model. Each configuration is stored with its evidence, so the provider can audit every deployment decision, including unmet requirements. Our evaluation with the KGW watermark shows that (i) on misuse-prone requests, the framework detects more paraphrased text than fixed configurations and random search at matching clean detection and quality, (ii) it exe

b0ffcabdf5c5cea0998baf51.title_original: Safe at One Loop, Risky at Another: Aligning Safety Across Recurrent Depths in Looped Language Models
b0ffcabdf5c5cea0998baf51.excerpt: arXiv:2610.10625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) provide a parameter efficient approach to scaling model capabilities through repeated use of shared parameters across recurrent steps. Since each recurrent depth can be read out independently, a single LoopLM exposes a broader output space across inference depths, raising an important question: whether safety is preserved throughout recurrent computation. Prior evaluations suggest that deeper recurrence can improve safety on harmful queries, but robustness under jailbreak attacks remains unclear. We therefore conduct a comprehensive safety evaluation of LoopLMs under jailbreak attacks targeting different recurrent depths. We find that attack success can increase at deeper inference depths, the same query can elicit different safety behaviors across depths, and attacks constructed against one depth can transfer to others. Moreover, SFT and preference alignment do not eliminate these safety gaps, motivating an alignment method designed for LoopLMs. We introduce SafeBridge, which combines lightweight depth specific control of shared recurrent layers, selective state bridging, and joint safety supervision across recurrent depths. Across model scales, multiple attack methods, and safety benchmarks, SafeBridge substantially reduces attack success for both matched-depth and cross-depth attacks. It also improves general utility over the vanilla models while maintaining comparable over-refusal behavio

f2ff4f85a065143d5640b7a1.title_original: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
f2ff4f85a065143d5640b7a1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21245v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of $\varepsilon$ may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. We categorize existing approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization. We analyze their underlying assumptions and privacy--utility trade-offs. Rather than ranking methods by $\varepsilon$ alone, we propose a framework that interprets a DP-RAG guarantee along three dimensions: privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries. We conclude that an $\eps$ is a claim only together with the three slots: the protected unit, the accounting scope, and the release boundary.

82c07f0f4751d0a8aecb1b5c.title_original: Memoir: Learning, Verifying, and Evolving False-Positive Memories for Static Application Security Testing Tools
82c07f0f4751d0a8aecb1b5c.excerpt: arXiv:2608.09181v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools have become indispensable in modern secure software devel- opment. However, these tools often generate false-positive (FP) alerts, imposing substantial manual inspection costs and reducing the trust from developers. Existing FP reduction methods still face two primary challenges. First, the large differences among SAST tools and vulnerability categories make it difficult for these methods to learn recurring patterns in historical false positives. Moreover, the knowledge used by these methods are largely static and cannot be updated as newly validated cases accumulate. To address these challenges, we propose Memoir, a memory- driven framework for identifying false positives by transform- ing historical FP alerts into reusable semantic memories. It consists of two key modules. First, historical semantic memory construction converts historical FP alerts into structured semantic memories through LLM-guided annotation, pattern clustering, and memory synthesis to capture reusable behavioral patterns. Moreover, memory-driven identification and evolution retrieves relevant memories and performs semantic verification against taxonomy consistency and security invariants before making the final prediction. It then incorporates verified predictions back into the memory repository, allowing the knowledge base to evolve as new cases accumulate. We evaluate Memoir on CWE- Bench-Java to

5e4e210c858b554c6304f79d.title_original: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
5e4e210c858b554c6304f79d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16770v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Next-generation wireless networks are expected to support high data rates and reliable connectivity while meeting requirements for energy efficiency, resource management, and communication security. Digital Twin (DT) technology represents expected network behavior and enables the actual network state to be assessed against it. Integrating DT technology with reinforcement learning (RL) supports adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) method for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network model. Receiver-level residuals between attack-free and attacked configurations are combined with candidate spatial jamming footprints and accumulated into a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into its state, reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. Compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs per configuration, with known jammer counts, BGQL achieves link-rate scores of 437.4-564.2 Mbit/s, rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37-76.79 Mbit/J, and localization recall of 100% for one jammer and 78%-81% for two jammers. BGQL requires 80-130 s per run versus 5-14 s for SARSA. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks

CVE-2026-115817.description: Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow a stalled request body to hold a worker indefinitely, as read_timeout covers only the headers. Content-Length and chunked request bodies are read with blocking reads and no deadline. A client that sends complete headers and then stalls or trickles the body keeps the worker waiting until it disconnects. A remote attacker can take every worker with a few such connections, five with the default worker count, so the server stops answering requests. Version 0.4019 applies read_timeout to each wait for body data and adds a body_timeout limit, 300 seconds by default, on the total time to read a body.
CVE-2026-115817.summary_ko: Starman의 요청 본문 처리 과정에서 read_timeout 미비로 인해 워커가 무한 대기 상태에 빠질 수 있습니다. 원격 공격자가 이를 악용해 서버의 모든 워커를 점유하여 서비스 거부 상태를 유발할 수 있습니다.

CVE-2026-115822.description: Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic regex backtracking when parsing chunked request bodies. Starman decodes chunked request bodies before calling the application, matching each chunk-size line with `s/^(([0-9a-fA-F]+).*\015\012)//`. A line of hex digits followed by a bare LF and then CRLF never matches, because `.` does not match LF, and each failed attempt backtracks in time quadratic in the length of the hex run. Nothing limits the length of the line. A remote attacker can exhaust worker CPU by sending such requests to any route.

CVE-2026-115823.description: Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl send response bodies for HEAD requests, desynchronizing responses on keep-alive connections. For a HEAD request Starman omits chunked framing but still writes the body returned by the application, on both the array and streaming response paths. Responses with a 1xx, 204 or 304 status also carry the body. On a keep-alive or pipelined connection the client reads those bytes as the start of the next response. A front-end proxy that reuses upstream connections may then pair responses with the wrong requests.

CVE-2026-115824.description: Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies. The chunked body decoder keeps each chunk in memory until the whole chunk and its CRLF have arrived, and sets no limit on the length of a chunk-size line. A client that declares a huge chunk size and streams data, or sends a chunk-size line that never ends, grows the buffer for as long as it keeps sending. A remote attacker can exhaust worker memory with a single connection.

CVE-2026-115825.description: HTTP::Server::PSGI versions before 1.0056 for Perl allow a single request to crash the server by declaring a large Content-Length. The request body is read with sysread() calls sized by the remaining Content-Length. Perl grows the read buffer to the requested length before any data arrives, so the server tries to allocate as much memory as the client declares. A remote attacker can send one request with a large Content-Length and a few body bytes, and perl exits with an out-of-memory error before the application is called. HTTP::Server::PSGI runs as a single process, so the server stays down until restarted.
CVE-2026-115825.summary_ko: HTTP::Server::PSGI에서 매우 큰 Content-Length 값을 가진 요청을 처리할 때 과도한 메모리를 할당하려는 시도로 인해 서버가 중단될 수 있습니다. 원격 공격자가 이 취약점을 이용해 메모리 부족 오류를 유발하고 서버를 다운시킬 수 있습니다.

CVE-2026-114214.description: Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash allows a client to read destination records unrelated to the source record through a through relationship. When a has_many relationship declared with through: was loaded for a single record with a limit of 1, or an unsorted has_one through relationship was loaded with a limit of 1, lateral_join?/4 in lib/ash/actions/read/relationships.ex chose the path that reads the destination without any filter linking it to the source. The load returned the first destination record by sort, or any other record with an offset. The read still runs the destination's policies but carries the relationship as accessing_from, so a client paging such a field (for example teachers(limit: 1, offset: n) through AshGraphql) can enumerate destination records that policies allow only when reached through that relationship. This issue affects ash: from 3.24.0 before 3.37.1.
CVE-2026-114214.summary_ko: ash-project의 ash 프레임워크에서 잘못된 권한 부여로 인해 원격 클라이언트가 소스 레코드와 연결되지 않은 대상 레코드를 열람할 수 있는 취약점이 발견되었습니다. 관계 로딩 시 필터링이 누락되어 인가되지 않은 데이터를 조회할 수 있습니다.

CVE-2026-115627.description: Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_postgres allows a user to load destination records linked to a source record only through another tenant's join rows. When a many_to_many relationship, or a through relationship, is loaded with a lateral join (for example with a per-record limit or sort), AshPostgres.DataLayer builds the query for the join resource, and for each resource along a through path, in lateral_join_query/3 and through_step_queries/4 without running that resource's read action, which is where attribute multitenancy is applied. When those resources use strategy :attribute multitenancy, rows belonging to other tenants were joined, so the load returned destination records that the caller's tenant is not related to. This issue affects ash_postgres: from 0.38.0 before 2.15.2.

CVE-2026-115635.description: Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_postgres allows a user to read another tenant's record through a skipped upsert. When Ash.bulk_create/4 or a single create runs as an upsert with return_skipped_upsert?: true and the upsert is skipped (for example because its upsert_condition does not hold), AshPostgres.DataLayer reads the existing row back by the upsert identity in do_bulk_create/3 and upsert/4. That lookup did not apply the resource's attribute multitenancy, so on a resource using strategy :attribute it could match and return the row of another tenant with the same identity values, exposing its fields to the caller. This issue affects ash_postgres: from 2.6.22 before 2.15.2.

CVE-2026-96581.description: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key vulnerability in ash-project ash allows a user of one tenant to read, overwrite and take over another tenant's records via an upserting create action. Under attribute multitenancy, Ash.Actions.Create (lib/ash/actions/create/create.ex) and Ash.Actions.Create.Bulk (lib/ash/actions/create/bulk.ex) upserted on the primary key, or on an all_tenants? identity, without scoping the conflicting record to the request's tenant. A caller of a create action with upsert? true that accepts the primary key, supplying a record id from another tenant, updated that record's upsert fields and received all of its attributes in the result. With the default upsert fields the tenant attribute was written too, moving the record into the caller's tenant. Read and update policies do not run for upserts, and tenant-scoped create policies pass because the tenant is the caller's own. This issue affects ash: from 1.22.0 before 3.37.2.
CVE-2026-96581.summary_ko: ash-project ash 프레임워크의 upsert 작업에서 테넌트 간 권한 우회 취약점이 발견되었습니다. 공격자가 타 테넌트의 레코드를 읽거나 덮어쓰고, 자신의 테넌트로 가져올 수 있습니다.

34c9221fc463201c3edadcf3.title_ko: SAMI Suite, 설치 없이 웹에서 바로 편집하는 무료 오피스 서비스 소개
34c9221fc463201c3edadcf3.summary_ko: 사미텍이 출시한 SAMI Suite는 별도의 소프트웨어 설치 없이 웹 브라우저에서 HWP, 워드, 엑셀, 파워포인트, PDF 문서를 열고 편집할 수 있는 무료 웹 오피스 도구입니다. 기존 로컬 문서 검색 도구인 Findex에 이어 사용자의 편의성을 높이기 위해 공개되었습니다.

e78fdcef4310cb89acb5fff3.title_ko: 메타, 개인용 AI 에이전트 '뮤즈'에 실시간 음성 대화 및 아바타 공유 기능 확대
e78fdcef4310cb89acb5fff3.summary_ko: 메타가 AI 에이전트 뮤즈(Muse)에 실시간 음성 대화 기능과 애니메이션 아바타 공유 기능을 추가하며 서비스 고도화에 나서고 있습니다. 또한 업무용 커넥터 확대와 더불어 데이터 보안을 강화하는 컨피덴셜 VM 및 고도화된 모델 '뮤즈 원더' 도입 등을 통해 일상과 업무 영역으로 영향력을 넓히고 있습니다.

a032fb4aadf215a29eaa8ccf.title_ko: Microsoft 365 겨냥한 AitM 기반 토큰 탈취 공격으로 79개 조직 피해
a032fb4aadf215a29eaa8ccf.summary_ko: 사이버 공격자들이 중간자(AitM) 공격을 통해 마이크로소프트 365 세션 토큰을 탈취하고 이를 재사용하여 79개 조직의 계정을 침해하는 사례가 보고되었습니다. 공격자는 다중 인증(MFA)을 우회하고 지속적인 접근을 위해 악성 기기를 등록하거나 이메일 규칙을 변조하여 정보를 탈취하고 있습니다.

1831334bfa97010609eccc67.title_ko: 오픈AI, 국내 스타트업 AI 서비스 개발 지원 프로그램 '모델 마스터즈' 개최
1831334bfa97010609eccc67.summary_ko: 오픈AI가 국내 스타트업의 AI 서비스 개발과 사업 현장의 문제 해결을 지원하기 위해 '오픈AI 모델 마스터즈'를 개최했습니다. 이번 행사에서는 11개 참여 기업이 오픈AI 모델을 활용한 업무 자동화, 영상 편집 솔루션 등 다양한 AI 활용 사례를 선보였으며, 컷백이 1위를 차지했습니다.

43bc421ee81ebd4e4048cd35.title_ko: 오픈AI와 앤트로픽, 가격 할인과 신모델 출시로 AI API 시장 경쟁 격화
43bc421ee81ebd4e4048cd35.summary_ko: 오픈AI가 적극적인 가격 할인과 무료 크레딧을 앞세워 기업 고객 확보에 나선 가운데, 앤트로픽은 고성능 신모델 출시를 통해 점유율을 방어하며 치열한 경쟁을 벌이고 있습니다. 고객사들은 가격 경쟁력과 모델 성능을 바탕으로 서비스 제공업체를 유연하게 변경하고 있어 향후 경쟁 구도는 더욱 복잡해질 전망입니다.

4fc5f21d9f4e28c9530e8630.title_ko: 솔트웨어, 생성형 AI 보안 솔루션 '사피가디언' 민감정보 탐지 특허 획득
4fc5f21d9f4e28c9530e8630.summary_ko: 솔트웨어가 생성형 AI 이용 시 정보 유출을 방지하는 '사피가디언'의 민감정보 탐지 및 제어 기술로 특허를 획득했습니다. 이 솔루션은 규칙 기반 탐지와 AI 문맥 분석을 결합해 기업의 보안 정책에 따라 민감 정보를 차단하거나 마스킹 처리하여 업무 효율성과 보안성을 동시에 지원합니다.

1b748d85801878668a0cc2e4.title_ko: 경찰청-씽크포비엘, AI 영향 평가 및 위험 관리 체계 구축
1b748d85801878668a0cc2e4.summary_ko: 경찰청이 씽크포비엘과 협력해 AI 기획부터 운영까지 전 과정을 관리할 수 있는 글로벌 수준의 위험 관리 체계를 마련했습니다. EU AI 법 및 국제 표준을 반영한 이 체계는 도입 적합성 판별, 신뢰성 검증, 운영 중단 조치 권한 등을 포함하며, 내년 법령 시행에 따른 공공기관의 AI 관리 의무에 대응할 계획입니다.

curation.reason_ko: 경찰청이 AI 도입 및 운영 전 과정의 위험을 관리하기 위해 씽크포비엘과 협력하여 체계를 마련했습니다.

187d364cfee09ef8348cb63d.title_ko: 아우토크립트, ITS 세계총회서 차량 보안 기술 발표
187d364cfee09ef8348cb63d.summary_ko: 아우토크립트가 ITS 세계총회 2026에서 C-ITS 보안 구축 사례와 전기차 충전 보안 기술을 공개했습니다. 또한, 2026년 11월 3일 한국과학기술회관에서 열리는 ‘인공지능 보안 컨퍼런스(AIS 2026)’가 개최될 예정이며, 관련 정보보호 실무자들은 사전 등록을 통해 참석할 수 있습니다.

7b2b6a1017ee4e610c3d8f4f.title_ko: 이디오그램, 편집 가능한 벡터 이미지 생성 AI 모델 공개
7b2b6a1017ee4e610c3d8f4f.summary_ko: 이디오그램(Ideogram)이 텍스트로 설명하면 SVG 파일을 생성하거나 기존 이미지를 벡터로 변환하는 AI 모델 ‘이디오그램 벡터’를 공개했습니다. 이 도구는 로고나 일러스트 등 디자인 작업 시 해상도 제약 없이 수정이 가능하며, 개발자를 위한 API 연동 기능도 함께 지원합니다.

8481ae162455cd518592c0d1.title_ko: 원티드랩, FDE 채용 박람회 개최 등 주요 단신
8481ae162455cd518592c0d1.summary_ko: 원티드랩이 11월 18일 잠실 롯데월드타워에서 2년 이상 경력 개발자를 대상으로 'FDE 리크루팅 카니발'을 개최하며 16일까지 참가자를 모집합니다. 이 외에도 단국대-팔로알토네트웍스 협력, SK텔레콤의 AI 거버넌스 리포트 발간, 경찰청의 AI 위험 관리 체계 도입 등 국내 AI 및 보안 관련 동향이 발표되었습니다.

aba464dbe3b800b4de371955.title_ko: 생성형 AI와 검색 엔진 교차 이용 행태 급증
aba464dbe3b800b4de371955.summary_ko: 챗GPT와 같은 생성형 AI의 확산에도 불구하고, 환각 우려로 인해 사용자들이 네이버·구글 등 기존 검색 엔진을 교차로 활용하는 사례가 크게 늘었습니다. 업계는 향후 검색 엔진이 생성형 AI 기능을 강화하고 AI 서비스는 검색 기능을 보완하며 두 서비스의 경계가 점차 허물어질 것으로 전망합니다.

85fafa2877cb09c970d14f44.title_ko: GitHub 토큰 탈취를 통한 비밀 정보 유출 공격 'Gheist' 주의
85fafa2877cb09c970d14f44.summary_ko: 공격자들이 탈취한 GitHub 토큰으로 개인 저장소에 악성 워크플로우를 삽입해 시크릿(비밀 정보)을 로그로 유출하는 'Gheist' 캠페인이 발견되었습니다. 보안 기업 Wiz는 피해 저장소 확인을 위해 ci-sync-로 시작하는 브랜치와 삭제된 워크플로우 실행 내역 등을 모니터링하고 비밀 정보를 즉시 교체할 것을 권고했습니다.

089ec78a63d18db0e4f005a2.title_ko: 미래에셋생명, 시스템 침해로 인한 고객 개인정보 유출 확인
089ec78a63d18db0e4f005a2.summary_ko: 미래에셋생명은 외부 침입으로 인해 일부 고객의 신용정보가 유출된 사실을 확인했다고 밝혔다. 보험업권에서 발생한 첫 해킹 사례로, 현재 회사는 외부 전문기관과 협력하여 정확한 유출 항목과 대상을 분석 중이다.

curation.reason_ko: 미래에셋생명에서 시스템 침해 사고가 발생하여 고객 신용정보가 유출되었습니다.

1fa65e89607bcbf97867eb92.title_ko: 자체 모델 기반 터미널용 AI 코딩 에이전트 '미르코드' 출시
1fa65e89607bcbf97867eb92.summary_ko: 터미널에서 직접 실행 가능한 TUI 기반 AI 코딩 에이전트 '미르코드(Mirr Code)'가 공개되었다. 이 도구는 프로젝트 내 코드 탐색 및 파일 수정 등 실질적인 개발 작업 수행을 목적으로 개발되었다.

summary.title_ko: 클라우드플레어, 다단계 보안 감사를 위한 'security-audit-skill' 공개
summary.summary_ko: 클라우드플레어(Cloudflare)가 공개한 'security-audit-skill'은 다단계 보안 감사를 수행하도록 설계된 코딩 에이전트용 기술입니다. 이 도구는 기계 판독이 가능한 감사 결과를 생성하고 이를 독립적으로 검증할 수 있도록 지원합니다.

summary.title_ko: 엔비디아(NVIDIA), 자율 AI 에이전트를 위한 오픈쉘(OpenShell) 공개
summary.summary_ko: 엔비디아가 자율형 AI 에이전트를 위한 안전하고 개인정보 보호가 강화된 런타임 환경인 OpenShell을 공개했습니다.
